passage: Darshan's night shifts at the hospital pharmacy meant he and Urmila overlapped for barely two hours a day, and most of their marriage happened by text. After last month's week-long sulk over a message that turned out to mean nothing, they sat on the balcony one Sunday and wrote two rules on a sticky note for the fridge. One: anything emotional waits for the 8 p.m. call before his shift, or Sunday breakfast. Two: if a text feels curt, the reply is a question, not a verdict. The test came on Wednesday. Darshan texted, 'Can't. Busy.' Urmila felt the old sting. Then she remembered who had written it: the man who left her tea in a flask every morning. She typed, 'All ok? 🤍' He replied an hour later: 'Sorry! Emergency order. Love you.'

qa.q: When does anything emotional get discussed, according to their first rule?
qa.a: It waits for the 8 p.m. call before his shift, or Sunday breakfast.

qa.q: Why was Urmila able to move past 'the old sting' on Wednesday?
qa.a: She remembered Darshan's loving intent, the man who left her tea in a flask every morning, and chose to read his text generously.

qa.q: Why do these two rules suit a couple with so little overlap?
qa.a: They keep hard feelings for moments when voices and time are available, and turn curt texts into questions, so busy-hour messages don't snowball.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel reading Urmila's question during an emergency?
qa.a: He probably feels cared for rather than accused, which makes it easy to explain and apologise once he's free.

passage: On the first Sunday of every month, Francis and Ankita had a ritual at the dining table of their Panaji flat: filter coffee, and a look back at the month's texts. Today Ankita scrolled to a Tuesday message of hers: 'do what you want.' Francis grinned. 'And I replied?' '"What does that mean?"' she read. 'Question, not a fight. Rule two.' They'd agreed on the rules after a bad spring: anything that hurt or mattered went to a phone call or the evening walk, never a paragraph over chat. And a short text got a question before a reaction. 'I was only exhausted that day,' Ankita said. 'I know,' said Francis. 'You love me too much to mean that.' She threw a cushion at him, laughing.

qa.q: What did Francis reply to 'do what you want'?
qa.a: 'What does that mean?'

qa.q: What does Francis's line 'You love me too much to mean that' show about how he reads Ankita?
qa.a: He reads her with generosity, remembering her love and intent rather than taking the curt words at face value.

qa.q: What makes their monthly look-back a useful habit?
qa.a: It lets them notice misreadings calmly, laugh at them, and keep practising their rules before small snowballs grow.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt on Tuesday when Francis asked instead of reacting?
qa.a: Probably relieved 😊, since her exhaustion was met with a question rather than a fight.

grounding: A couple review their texts monthly, keeping emotional topics for calls or walks and meeting curt texts with questions, reading each other generously.

Wasim groaned. "We're writing rules?"

After the text fight in March, Pradeep and I sat on the balcony and made two rules. Looking back, they've saved us more than once.
One: anything emotional, we call or keep it for the evening. No arguing in text.
Two: if a message feels curt, I don't decide what it means. I ask.
Last week it was tested. He texted "not now" when I sent him the flat-hunting links. Old me, the girl who read every short message as a verdict, would have sulked for a day. I just wrote, "Busy?" He replied, "Client on the line. Love the second flat. Talk tonight."
It's not magic. It's just remembering the person on the other end loves me. I'm Shalini, and I'm still learning to read kindly.

qa.q: What did Pradeep text when Shalini sent the flat-hunting links?
qa.a: "Not now."

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when she chose to write "Busy?"
qa.a: She felt calm and trusting enough to ask instead of sulking, remembering that he loves her.

qa.q: Which rule helped most last week, and why?
qa.a: Asking instead of deciding what a curt message meant, because it showed Pradeep was simply on a client call.

qa.q: What does the second rule mean for Pradeep?
qa.a: Pradeep's short texts get a question instead of a sulk, so he has a chance to explain.

grounding: Shows a couple's agreed norms, emotional talks by call or in the evening and a question for curt texts, preventing a snowball.

Counsellor's note, third session
Tushar and Lata arrived with a sheet of paper today, their own idea. After last month's text fight, which pulled in both their families, they wrote "our rules":
1. Emotional topics: call, or wait for the evening.
2. A short text gets a question, not a reaction.
3. Assume the other meant well.
They said they'd already used rule two twice. Lata described a curt message from Tushar and said she wrote "Rough day?" instead of "What's your problem?". Tushar laughed and said, "It was. Thank you."
The warmth between them was clearer today. Next session I will ask how the rules hold up during a busy week.
Harsha

qa.a: Assume the other meant well.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he laughed and said "Thank you"?
qa.a: He seemed relieved and grateful that Lata asked about his day instead of reacting.

qa.q: Why is Harsha planning to ask about a busy week?
qa.a: Because rules are easiest when life is calm; a busy week tests whether they read each other generously under stress.

qa.q: How does Lata seem to experience the new rules?
qa.a: Lata seems proud and more at ease, describing how asking "Rough day?" changed the outcome.

grounding: Shows a counsellor's note on a couple's rules: emotional talks by call or evening, questions for curt texts, and generous reading.

Thursday, 11 p.m.
Ira and I finally did the thing we keep talking about. We wrote rules on the back of the electricity bill envelope, now stuck to the fridge.
1. Anything that feels heavy gets a phone call, or waits for the evening. Not text.
2. If one of us sends something short and cold, the other replies with a question, not a matching short line. "Rough day?" is allowed. "Fine." is not.
3. Assume the other meant well until you've asked.
We tested it by five o'clock. Ira's message: "Can't do Saturday." Old me would have written "ok." and sulked till dinner. I wrote, "Rough day? What happened?" Ira called from the office stairwell: "Jaya, they changed my Saturday shift without telling anyone." Two minutes, done.
It felt a bit silly and a bit wonderful. Married two years, and still learning to read each other.

qa.q: Where did Jaya and Ira write their rules?
qa.a: On the back of the electricity bill envelope, now stuck to the fridge.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel after the first test of the rules?
qa.a: Jaya felt a bit silly and a bit wonderful, pleased and relieved that one question settled things in two minutes.

qa.q: Why does answering a curt text with a question help?
qa.a: A question invites the real reason, like the changed shift, instead of trading cold lines and guessing.

qa.q: What was it like for Ira to get "Rough day? What happened?"
qa.a: Ira could explain the changed shift at once instead of facing a cold reply, which likely felt like being supported.

grounding: Shows a couple agreeing that emotional topics go to a call or the evening and that a curt text gets a question, then trying it the same day.
